text: A tune on a violin turns Curly into a fighter, and stopping the tune turns him off again. That is the entire engine, and seventeen minutes is about as long as such an engine can run before it seizes. Moe hears the mechanism first, in a restaurant, and does what a manager does: books the bouts and keeps the fiddler close, which makes Larry less a musician than a piece of equipment that has to be transported to the arena intact. So the comedy is really about supply — one song, one player, one instrument made of wood, against a fight schedule that assumes all three will hold. It sits on the National Film Registry, an odd berth for a knockabout two-reeler whose logic belongs to a physics problem more than to a plot.

The number is written on his forehead: 9413, ink where a name should be. Fourteen minutes is a strange length for a career, and the compression is the point — the arrival, the waiting, the conversion of a face into a piece of paperwork, with none of the consoling detail a feature would supply. Slavko Vorkapich made it in 1928, inside the industry it describes, in a town whose product was the star's name above the title. This film withholds the name. What it offers instead is design: an experiment in telling a story of ambition through shape, light and rhythm rather than through a person the audience is allowed to know. The National Film Registry keeps it, which means Hollywood preserved the small hard thing made at its own expense.

Two pressures reach Tommy Turner in the same weekend, and the film declines to rank them: a trustee who has already forced three teachers out over suspected communism, and Joe Ferguson, football hero and his wife's old sweetheart, arriving for homecoming. The passage of prose Tommy means to read aloud in class is the kind of small act that costs a job. Ellen would rather he skipped it, and that stings worse than the threat. An American campus comedy from 1942, then, with teeth showing through the jokes: a marriage tested by a pep rally, a career tested by a paragraph, all of it while everyone around them enjoys the weekend. The National Board of Review placed it among the year's ten best. Its nerve is in making the loyalty panic a domestic argument, conducted at home, in front of a guest.

A man asks the warden not to release him, and then explains, at length, why he is better off inside. Andrzej Munk's 1960 film takes the request seriously enough to follow the account all the way back, through a middle-aged Polish life recounted as one long chain of misfortune, most of it spent trying to fit in with whoever happened to be in charge that year. The comedy is dry and it accumulates. He tells his humiliations with the steady pride of a man who has at least been consistent, and the case he assembles is against himself. Zezowate szczęście keeps a place in the Polish canon. The pattern it draws is not really about luck, and the film is funniest at the moments when its narrator is at his most agreeable.

Seven years after Hiroshima, an American studio made a picture about the man who flew the plane, and made his hesitation the subject. Colonel Paul Tibbets trains for a weapon he has not been told the whole truth about; he knows only that it will kill on a scale nothing before it managed, and two hours go to the weight of that partial knowledge rather than to the mission itself. The interesting stretch is the interval before — how long a man can carry an order he doubts and still carry it, while the pressure on him only increases. It took the Academy Award for Best Story, a curious prize for events its first audience had followed in the papers. Made in 1952, the film stands closer to the event than to us, and its unease reads differently for that.

Bunker Hill, Los Angeles, one night in 1961: rooming houses on a slope above downtown, and the young Native men and women who had left reservations to live in them. Kent MacKenzie gives it seventy-two minutes, roughly the length of a night's aimlessness — bars, cars, the walking between them, the hours in which nothing is decided and everybody keeps moving anyway. Holding to a single night is what gives the film its edge: no arc of arrival, no explanations offered to an outsider, only the texture of time passed a long way from where these people came from and not quite anywhere else yet. The National Film Registry keeps it. What has been preserved is less an argument than an address — a particular set of streets, and the sound of people spending an evening on them.

The evidence against Henry Reyna was, in large part, his clothes. Luis Valdez adapted his own play about the Sleepy Lagoon case, in which a group of young Mexican-Americans is sent to San Quentin on a record that barely holds together, and he did not sand the theatre off in the transfer: the songs stay, the diction stays heightened, the film lets itself be watched as a performance while the case underneath it remains a matter of documented fact. Part invention, part record, and the seam is deliberately visible. Alice Bloomfield and George Shearer work the defense from outside the cell; inside, young men learn how fast a way of dressing becomes a prosecution theory. The National Film Registry keeps it, a strange destination for a picture from 1981 that never stops sounding like a stage.

A gambler twenty dollars short at the betting window leaves his small daughter as security. The bookie takes her, because a marker is a marker, and the film proceeds from that piece of arithmetic with more nerve than the sweetness around it would suggest. Its New York — Big Steve's Horseshoe Cabaret, a race arranged to be lost, men named for their dispositions — is an environment in which a child is an item held against a debt, and the comedy comes from grown men adjusting to that fact rather than from anyone being adorable. Sorrowful Jones has a fix to protect and no interest in custody. Bangles Carson, singing at the club, has better instincts and less authority. Seventy-nine minutes, 1934, and the joke it is built on stays cold longer than the genre usually allows.

A preacher gives away what little the household has; his son wants to cut into bodies and be paid for it. Of Human Hearts sets that quarrel in a poor congregation in the years before the Civil War, where the difference between tending a soul and setting a bone is also a difference about money, and about what a family owes the town it serves. Clarence Brown directs it as a domestic chronicle rather than a war picture — the fighting comes, but the pressure is applied at the table, over schooling and debts, with the mother standing between the two men. The performance in that role took the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress. What lasts is the sourness the film permits a son to feel toward a good man, and how long it lets him hold on to it.

The plot is a formality and the film knows it: an American heiress, an Argentine horse breeder, two families opposed, and then the numbers begin. Down Argentine Way was assembled in 1940 to be looked at — Technicolor, location footage, a design scheme that took an Academy Award for its handling of colour — and the romance exists mostly to carry everyone from one performance to the next. Carmen Miranda sings South American Way. The Nicholas Brothers dance. Neither has much bearing on the love story, and neither needs any. What the picture is chiefly doing is arranging an Argentina for North American eyes, and it makes no pretence otherwise; the National Film Registry keeps it as a record of that arrangement, and of what colour looked like while the process was still new.

Ninety minutes with Thelonious Monk, most of them spent watching a band work rather than explaining the man at the piano. Charlotte Zwerin built the film around performance footage and put the interviews where they belong, at the edges: friends and family describing someone they plainly loved and did not entirely follow. What comes through is how much of this music is labour — a tempo found, a tune run again, musicians waiting while somebody decides something. The talk offers affection and puzzlement, not a diagnosis. The camera stays with Monk in a room and never asks him to perform being interesting. It is on the National Film Registry, and the reason is restraint: the hardest move available to a music documentary is to stop narrating and let the take run to its end.

There was no camera in the water, so Winsor McCay drew it. Twelve minutes of animation, made in 1918, reconstructing the torpedoing of an ocean liner that no newsreel had been present to film, and made to keep American anger at Germany at a useful temperature. The technique does double work: drawing here is not a cartoon idiom but a stand-in for evidence, a way of putting an audience beside a ship that exists only in ink. Smoke, water, the slow tilt of a hull, produced line by line with the patience of a draughtsman and the purpose of a recruiting poster. The National Film Registry holds it, which suits a piece of persuasion obliged to manufacture its own footage. Whether that manufacture makes the case stronger or weaker is left sitting in the room.

Flight, in 1924, meant wires, darkness and a camera willing to lie carefully. That is much of the pleasure here: Never Never Land has to be built out of paint, rope and trick photography, and every effect is achieved in front of the audience rather than around it. Herbert Brenon begins where the story always begins, in a nursery, with children invited to leave home by a boy who lets himself in — and silence suits the material, since Peter's appeal is a matter of gesture and dare rather than of argument. A hundred and one minutes is a long stretch for a nursery tale, and the film spends it on pirates, on the sea, on Captain Hook treating children as serious adversaries. On the National Film Registry, it survives as stage magic that admits what it is and works regardless.

The first feature shot in three-strip Technicolor is about a woman whose entire method is presentation, which was either luck or good sense. Rebecca Sharp has no money and no family; she takes a governess post and works upward through the drawing rooms of early nineteenth-century England, where dress is a claim about rank and rank is the only currency anyone respects. Rouben Mamoulian uses the new process to sort a room — who is dressed to be seen, who is dressed to be trusted — so the colour is not an ornament laid over a costume picture but the means of reading the costumes. Eighty-four minutes is quick for a long novel, and the compression suits a heroine who never stays anywhere long. The Academy Award for Best Actress went to the performance in the title role.
